episode_thesis: Jan van Eck argues that outside forces (fiscal and monetary policy, deregulation, technology, demographics, war) shape markets, so he builds portfolios from those forces rather than from market-internal theory, and reads every long backtest with the 40-year falling-rate regime in mind. In practice he stays fully invested in equities except when the Fed tightens aggressively, replaces part of the bond sleeve with real assets, rebalances, diversifies internationally (India above all), and uses valuation only as a secondary check inside a trend.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are embedded in a larger world: fiscal policy, monetary policy, money printing, technology and war shape financial markets, so portfolios should start from those forces, not from CAPM-style market-internal laws.
worldview_premises.support: Inherited philosophy from his father's firm (1955); contrast with academic finance; no data offered.

worldview_premises.premise: Skepticism toward official actions is part of the method; every investor has a personality bias (his is optimism, his father's was questioning) and should know it.

worldview_premises.premise: Very long trends (demographics above all) are priced slowly, so a multi-decade time lens is the most valuable filter for the daily information flow, although the investment implication of a trend is a separate question.
worldview_premises.support: China shrinking from about 1.5bn to 700-750m in 100 years, India now most populous.

worldview_premises.premise: The 40-year fall in US rates (early 1980s to about 1% in COVID) was a one-regime tailwind to bonds and stocks that is probably over, so any 40-year chart or backtest carries a falling-rates/inflation bias.
worldview_premises.support: Description of US long-term rate history; no quantification.

worldview_premises.support: Hong Kong trip in 1992 anecdote; notes private firms say little about their moats.

worldview_premises.premise: Basic institutional rules set the risk-taking regime: the Fed's biggest pre-crisis error was allowing mortgages with almost no money down, which biased risk-taking because borrowers risked little of their own money.
worldview_premises.support: Historical example of the housing run-up; asserted as under-discussed.

worldview_premises.premise: Old monetary data relationships are unreliable because lending has moved from banks to non-bank lenders, but one can still tell whether Fed and Treasury are stimulating or tightening.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets can miss big forces despite efficiency because humans imagine the future by looking backward; analysts cannot imagine trillion-dollar firms growing earnings 80-100% a year.

worldview_premises.premise: Government bond markets and pegged currencies are the most manipulated or paradigm-stuck markets; disconnects can persist and he does not understand them.

worldview_premises.premise: Because the world keeps changing, fixed rules are hard to write; he biases allocation using evidence across cycles and admits there is very little science behind his weights.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 60-70% equity / 10% real assets / rest bonds allocation is explicitly unsupported ('very little science').

Says he does not use valuation at market or industry level but then cites valuation extremes in Nvidia, SpaceX, alt managers and international markets; he concedes there is no great answer to value versus trend.
Gold is called the best resilience asset against spending concerns, yet he says it falls with everything in a confidence shock; the conditions that favour gold are not specified.
Says patterns do not always give a signal and technology is hardest to turn into a signal, but gives no rule for when a pattern is actionable.
The rule 'worry when the Fed hikes sharply' is illustrated by a single 2022 episode with no threshold defined beyond 1% to 4%.
Does not understand government bond market disconnects and missed the early 1990s currency breakup; macro framework gives no guidance on rates or FX.
Optimism bias is admitted, yet bullish calls (India, international, Nvidia moat) are made without stating how the bias is controlled.
Retail-behaviour claim (individuals show bad habits, institutions do not) is anecdotal.
Sell-side under-forecasting of extreme earnings growth is asserted without data.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Stated drivers of future prices: US fiscal deficit size (about 6% of GDP as stimulus), Fed stance (rapid tightening is the equity warning; inflation limits cuts), deregulation and digitization in India, technology market structure and moats (Nvidia ecosystem), policy-driven demand for nuclear/power, supply-constrained copper and metals, Bitcoin halving cycle, valuation extremes in narrative stocks (price-to-sales) and de-rated alt managers, and liquidity scrambles that sell gold and Treasuries. Horizons are mostly multi-year, with rebalancing quarterly.
reader_inferences: (reader) His 'fully invested unless the Fed is jamming rates' rule is effectively a single-state macro filter on equity exposure, with valuation and sentiment as secondary overlays rather than signals.

(reader) He treats macro as pattern recognition among four recurring patterns (deregulation, fiscal policy, monetary regime, technology), none of which he claims to have tested; it is a framework for allocation tilts rather than a trading signal.

(reader) The advocacy of India, international diversification and real assets is consistent with his firm's product lineup (semiconductor ETF, gold, commodities), a possible commercial bias he partly acknowledges ('I'm biased' on active funds).

(reader) The liquidation-in-stress mechanism and the 60/40 correlation premise are linked: if the stock-bond correlation turns positive in a rate-shock regime, real assets and gold may diversify only outside cash-scramble episodes.
